Dylan counted the boxes in the living room of apartment 4B. Nine were still taped shut, and his mother had given him until Sunday night, two days away, to unpack the ones with his name on them. Through the wall he could hear the family in 4C, the neighbours he had not met yet, and somewhere below that a dog barked at something he would never see.

Three weeks ago, in his old town, he had stood on Jasraj's porch and promised they would message every single day. They had managed eleven days. Then Jasraj's team made the playoffs and Dylan's messages sat unanswered for hours, and he had typed something sharp about friends who forget people. Jasraj typed back a single word: "Wow." Dylan had inhaled to reply with something worse, then put the phone face down on his desk instead. Neither of them had written since. Calling it a fight felt too big. Calling it nothing felt too small.

In the mail room on Friday he found a girl from 4C sitting on the recycling bin, holding a photograph of a street with tall trees and holding back tears at the same time. "We moved here Tuesday," she said, wiping her face with her sleeve. "It's homesickness," Dylan said. "That's what it's called, being away from home and your people." She looked at him like he had recited a spell. "Does it stop?" He did not know yet, so he said, "Ask me Sunday."

He had a reason to say that. He had been running a quiet experiment on himself, keeping notes in the back of a notebook. Week one, he had wanted to cry at the smell of his grandmother's soup, which his mother had finally made right. Week two, he had still thought about Jasraj at recess but had also learned the shortcut to the corner store. Something was fading, not all at once, more the way a bruise fades. Maybe homesickness worked like that for everyone, easing as you settled in. He wanted proof before he answered the girl.

Saturday afternoon he heard a thump against his door. It was the girl, and a boy from 4C named Stephen, playing hallway football with a rolled-up sock. "You're the endangered one," Stephen announced, pointing at Dylan's feet, which were bare sock territory. Dylan laughed before he could stop himself, a real laugh, the first one in this building. "Truce if you play," the girl offered, holding out the sock like a treaty. He took it. They played until a neighbour on the third floor banged on her ceiling.

Sunday night, boxes unpacked with eleven minutes to spare, Dylan knocked on 4C. The girl opened the door, sock still in hand. "It took me about three weeks to feel better," he said. "Yours might be faster. Or not. But it goes." She nodded slowly, then held up her phone. On the screen was a photo of her new street, bare little trees and all. "I took it today," she said. "For later."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
story:
Paisley taped the last photo to the display board at the community centre: a fishing crew on a wide grey bay, a woman in a embroidered parka, a cluster of houses under snow. Her group had one caption left to type, and the deadline was four o'clock.

"Read it back," said Ananya, who was typing on the laptop.

"An Inuit hunter from the photograph, taken in 1962," Ashwin read off the screen.

Paisley frowned. Something about it snagged in her mind, the way a thread catches on a splinter. She had seen the word used differently somewhere, but she could not place where. "Wait. Don't print yet."

"Why?" Ashwin said. "It's due in an hour."

"Because 'Inuit' is the word for a whole group of people. I think. It's like saying 'a French' instead of 'a French person.'" She could not explain how she knew; she had maybe read it on a museum plaque last summer, or heard it at her cousin's school assembly. She needed to check, and the school library was closed on Saturdays.

Ms. Zhou, who ran the community centre's weekend program, was setting out juice and crackers down the hall. Paisley went to find her, passing the smell of wet paint from the art room, and the squeak of sneakers from the gym where a badminton game was going on.

"Ms. Zhou, do you know if it's 'an Inuit' or something else, for one person?"

Ms. Zhou pulled out her phone. "My sister teaches up north. Let me look at her messages." She scrolled, then turned the screen. There it was, in a text about a school pen-pal project: the word Inuit means "the people" in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.

"An Inuk," Paisley said out loud, testing it. That was the missing piece, and it fit the pattern she had half-remembered: the group word and the single word were different, like the threads of the embroidery, whole cloth versus one stitch.

Back at the board, she changed the caption to "An Inuk hunter from the photograph." Ananya printed it, and Ashwin taped it beneath the picture of the man in the kayak.

At three fifty, a woman stopped in front of the display. She was wearing a pin shaped like an ulu, the curved knife Paisley had learned about while researching the fishing photos. The woman read the caption, then looked at the girls.

"You got it right," she said. "Most people don't." She tapped the frame. "That's my father in the kayak."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars called ofrendas with photos and marigolds, whose color and scent are said to guide spirits home.
story:
Declan stood in his grandma's kitchen for the first time since March, when everything had happened. The house still smelled like her coffee, and that was the problem. His dad was sorting boxes in the living room, and Declan wanted to say goodbye to her somehow, but he didn't know how, and the funeral had happened while he was sick with something contagious and running a fever, so he had never gotten the chance.

"Obstruct the doorway and I'll drop this box," his dad said, so Declan moved. He wandered to the fridge, where her magnets still held a grocery list in her handwriting. Stuck behind the list was a folded page addressed to him. He pulled it free and read it at the table.

"Dear Declan. If you are reading this at the house, then check the cupboard above the stove, the one I never let you open because of the good dishes. Yours is the box marked with a D. Love, Grandma." He got a chair, climbed up, and found a small box. Inside was a sugar skull she had painted with his name, orange and yellow, and a note that said only, "Ask Annie about November."

He texted Annie a photo of the skull. She called back in a minute. "My family does that," she said. "It's called an ofrenda. During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars with photos and marigolds. The color and the scent are said to guide spirits home. It's November 2 today, so if you're going to do it, it's today." Declan thought about that. He couldn't see whether any of it was true, but he could test it the only way available: he could build one and see how it felt to sit beside it.

Annie showed up twenty minutes later with a paper bag of marigolds from the store where Mr. Reddy was working the register on weekends. "He gave me an extra bunch when I told him," she said. On the porch table they set the sugar skull, her framed photo from the mantel, and one of her coffee mugs. The petals Declan scattered in a line from the front door toward the photo, because if the scent was supposed to guide her home, then the path should start where she would come in. Annie argued the petals should go in a circle instead, so they compromised: a path with a circle at the end, like a little landing pad.

They sat until the porch light came on. Nothing visibly arrived, but the smell of marigolds mixed with the smell of coffee still drifting from the kitchen, and Declan told Annie about the time his grandma had called a raccoon a carnivore and then chased it off her bird feeder with a broom. Annie laughed until she had to put her head on the table. Then the wind moved the petals slightly, all together, like something had walked through.

"Okay," Declan said quietly to the photo. "Hi, Grandma."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: Hens lay eggs whether or not a rooster is present; without a rooster the eggs are unfertilized and cannot hatch into chicks.
story:
The bus smelled like sunscreen and peanut butter sandwiches as it rattled up a gravel lane toward the Hartwell Homestead, a historic farm where people in old-fashioned clothes worked the land the way settlers had done almost two hundred years ago. Sydney pressed her forehead to the window. The farmhouse was tall and faded, with a porch swing that creaked even in the light wind, and behind it stood a barn, a garden, and a fenced yard where hens scratched in the dirt.

"The hens get to wander all day," Reed said, leaning across the aisle. "Lucky. Our class hamster just sits there."

Ms. Popescu, their guide for the day, met them at the gate wearing a long gray dress and a white apron. She explained that the homestead showed how a family lived in the 1830s, from the sparse furnishings in the sleeping loft to the heavy iron pots in the kitchen. Sydney noticed that almost everything in the farmhouse had a job, and often two. A bench was also a storage chest. A ladder was also a drying rack for herbs.

Then came the part Sydney had been waiting for. A costumed farmer let the students gather eggs from the nesting boxes along the henhouse wall. The straw smelled warm and dusty, and one brown hen squawked and flapped when Sydney reached beneath her, but the egg was there, smooth and heavier than she expected.

Reed held his egg up to the light and frowned. "Wait. Will this hatch? I haven't seen a single rooster anywhere. Not one, all morning."

Sydney thought about that. She had been watching the yard, too, and Reed was right, there were no roosters, only hens, maybe fifteen of them. But the nesting boxes had been full of eggs anyway, and the farmer had collected them in a basket for the kitchen, not for hatching. She turned her egg over in her hands, wondering. Maybe the hens didn't need a rooster to lay eggs at all. But if that were true, then an egg with no rooster around would never become a chick. She raised her hand.

"Excuse me," she said to the farmer. "The hens here lay eggs even with no rooster, right? So these eggs can't hatch into chicks?"

"That's it exactly," the farmer said, nodding. "We keep only hens at this yard, so the eggs are unfertilized. Good for eating, no chicks coming from them."

"So to get chicks," Reed said slowly, "you'd need a rooster somewhere."

Sydney grinned and tucked her egg carefully into the basket. Somewhere across the yard, a hen burst out of the barn door flapping her wings, and the whole class turned to look.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Studies of youth sports have found that players born early in the selection year are picked for teams more often than those born late, which researchers call the relative age effect.
story:
The gym smelled like floor wax and sweat, and Lea tied her shoes tighter before the second day of tryouts. She had played fine yesterday, she thought, but the coach kept stopping to watch her, and she wondered what he was writing on that clipboard. Maybe nothing. Maybe everything.

During the water break, Brennan leaned against the bleachers. "You see the list the coach taped to the door? Practice squad names go up Friday." Lea hadn't seen it, but she'd heard the eighth graders talking, and something they said had snagged in her mind like a sock on a nail. Every kid they mentioned seemed to have a birthday right after hers, in January or February. Was that a coincidence, or a pattern?

She decided to test it. "Brennan, when's your birthday?" He blinked. "March third. Why?" She moved down the line asking everyone the same question, keeping a mental tally on her fingers like a coach keeping stats. When they formed shooting lines, she counted the older kids in each one and quietly began to monitor which players the coach pulled aside for extra drills. Almost all of them were born early in the year. Nelson, who'd made the team last season, was a September birthday, but he was the tallest kid in the school, which she guessed didn't hurt.

At lunch she found Nelson in the library and explained her tally. He listened with his sandwich halfway to his mouth. "You counted birthdays?" "Half the gym," she said. "Most of the kids who get picked are months older than me. I'm December." Nelson wiped his hands and typed something on the library computer, scrolling, frowning. Then he turned the screen toward her. "Look. Studies of youth sports found that players born early in the selection year get picked more often than players born late. Researchers call it the relative age effect." Lea read the sentence twice. It had a name. It was a real thing, not just her imagination, and something about that made her feel less like a bad player and more like a mystery that hadn't been solved yet.

Still, she felt a flicker of skepticism. Maybe the older kids were simply better, pattern or no pattern. So she designed her own small experiment. At Friday's tryout she decided to count only her own results: made shots, completed passes, loose balls she reached first. Ten minutes in, she had hit seven of nine from the free throw line, and the coach had twice said her name in a voice that sounded like a good sign.

When the list went up, she stood on tiptoe behind Brennan to read it. There, in the middle of the practice squad, printed small and even: Lea. She read it again to be sure, then bounced once on the balls of her feet. "Told you," Nelson said from behind her. "Now quit blocking the door."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
story:
The nagar kirtan filled Penelope's whole street with orange. Her little brother rode on her dad's shoulders, and the smell of fried dough drifted from the langar tent at the end of the block. Penelope had invited her classmate Brynlee, who had never been to a Vaisakhi parade before, and Brynlee kept asking questions Penelope could not answer.

"So why is this day such a big deal?" Brynlee asked as a float rolled past with a canopy of yellow flowers.

Penelope opened her mouth and then closed it. She knew it had something to do with a Guru and something that started a long time ago, but she could not put the pieces together. She had a guess, that it was just a harvest festival like the autumn fair, but her guess felt thin. She decided to test it against the one person who always had answers.

"Come on," she said, and pulled Brynlee toward the front of the procession, where her uncle walked beside the truck carrying the Guru Granth Sahib under its embroidered canopy.

A boy about seven years old beat them to it. He tugged the uncle's sleeve and asked, "Why does everybody keep saying today matters?"

"Because in 1699, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," the uncle said. "That's the community of initiated Sikhs. Vaisakhi is the day we remember it." He straightened the boy's little turban and kept walking.

Penelope felt her harvest-festival guess fall apart. The parade was not just a party; it was a birthday, sort of, the birthday of the Khalsa itself. She turned it over while a drummer passed them, then another, and she spotted Markus from her class handing out cups of water. He would contradict her the second she got a detail wrong, so she practiced on him first.

"Markus, did you hear why today matters?"

"In 1699, the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," Markus said. "I asked your uncle twenty minutes ago. He told me twice because I forgot Anandpur."

So it held up. Penelope found Brynlee again by the langar tent, where volunteers were laying out paper plates. "I figured it out," she said. "It's not only a harvest thing. Vaisakhi is the day Sikhs remember 1699, when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur."

"Credible," Brynlee said, "for someone who just learned it five minutes ago."

"I heard it, I checked it, and Markus agreed," Penelope said. "That counts."

They got in line for food. Ahead of them, an old man who had been complaining to a volunteer about the crowd suddenly smiled and said, "Our landlord is over there serving chole, and last month he claimed he was too busy for anyone."

"Everyone's busy today anyway," the volunteer said, ladling out another bowl.

Penelope handed Brynlee a plate and pointed at the float turning the corner, flowers swaying. "Watch this part. This is the best bit of the whole parade."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologists distinguish forgiving, which means letting go of resentment, from reconciling, which means rebuilding the relationship; a person can forgive someone without the friendship returning to exactly how it was.
story:
The rain gauge on the park gazebo read zero, but Chloe checked the sky anyway, because the forecast had promised precipitation by five o'clock and her whole plan needed dry weather. She had exactly forty minutes to fix things with Skye before the storm and before the Friendship Day picnic ended, which was a terrible deadline for something nobody could really schedule.

The fight was three weeks old. Skye had told Mariana that Chloe's volcano project looked like "a melted birthday cake," which it did, but that was not the point. Chloe had heard it secondhand, stopped sitting with Skye at lunch, and the silence had hardened like old glue. Today, though, Chloe was ready to try, because her mom had said something on the drive over that Chloe kept turning over like a stone in her pocket.

"I forgive her," Chloe had told her mom in the car. "But I'm not ready to be best friends again yet. Is that allowed?"

"Totally," her mom had said, eyes on the road. "Forgiving is letting go of the resentment. It doesn't mean you're reconciling."

Chloe had looked the word up on her phone at the picnic table. Reconciling meant rebuilding the relationship, like putting a bridge back up plank by plank. So there were two separate things, not one. You could drop the heavy bag of being mad and still take your time walking back across the bridge. That felt consistent with how her chest actually felt, lighter but cautious, and it gave her an idea she could test.

She found Skye at the horseshoe pit, defending her title against Mariana. Chloe walked up, held out a paper plate with two cookies on it, and said, "Truce. But I'm warning you, I'm only reconciling at, like, medium speed."

Skye took a cookie and squinted at her. "What does that even mean?"

"It means I forgive you, so I'm not mad anymore. But the friendship has to rebuild itself. You can't rush a bridge." Chloe took a bite of her own cookie. "Also, my volcano did look like a melted birthday cake. I'm just saying you could have advocated for me instead of laughing."

Mariana raised her hand. "I would like it noted that I never laughed. I said it looked like modern art."

"You said it looked like a horror movie," Skye said.

"I said it looked like a horror movie with heart."

Skye set down her horseshoe. "Okay, medium speed. But can medium speed include the three-legged race? It starts in ten minutes and Mariana ties the knot too tight and cuts off my circulation."

Chloe pretended to consider it, tapping the cookie against her chin while the first fat drops of rain darkened the gazebo roof across the park. The precipitation had arrived early, which meant the race would be moved under the pavilion, which meant crowded concrete, which meant Skye would definitely stumble and blame Chloe's left leg, as she had every year since third grade.

"Medium speed includes the race," Chloe said, "if you admit my left leg is not the problem."

Skye stuck out her hand. "Your left leg is not the problem. Your left leg is a victim of my hopping."

They shook on it, and then Mariana pulled them both toward the pavilion, shouting, "Team Melted Cake, let's move!"

By the time they reached the starting line, the rain was drumming on the roof and Skye was already hopping.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: The 2019 Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right.
story:
Florence stood at the front of Room 12 with her hands folded behind her back, waiting for the word that might knock her out. Last year she had lost on "gneiss" in the third round, and for weeks afterward that silent letter had followed her around like a plague, showing up in her dreams and on cafeteria menus. This year she had studied every night, and now only she and Gary were left, the final two spellers in the class bee.

"Your word is 'chrysanthemum,'" said Ms. Ionescu.

Florence traced the letters in her mind, found the tricky spot, and spelled it slowly, the way a careful person crosses a river on stepping stones. Ms. Ionescu nodded. Then Gary spelled "rhinoceros" without even pausing, which struck Florence as reckless, like driving past a sign that said BRIDGE OUT. Round after round went by like that. Clarissa, watching from the second row, whispered something to the boy beside her, and Florence noticed it, because Clarissa never whispered during bees.

At lunch, Florence found out why. "Gary told me he wants to prolong the bee on purpose," Clarissa said, tearing her sandwich in half. "He read that in 2019, the Scripps National Spelling Bee ended with eight co-champions, because the spellers kept getting every word right. They ran out of words, I guess. Gary thinks if we all keep getting them right, Ms. Ionescu will have to make us co-champions too."

Florence turned this over all through math. Eight winners. A national bee, on a real stage, with eight champions because nobody missed. It had never occurred to her that a bee could end that way, that winning did not require someone else to lose. She thought about last year, when she had whispered "g-n-e-i-s-s" and watched Ravi celebrate. She had wanted him to miss. That wanting had felt ugly even then, and she had done it anyway.

Back in the classroom for the final rounds, she tested the idea. She spelled "vermilion" correctly, watching Ms. Ionescu flip to the next card. Gary spelled "belligerent." She spelled "facetious." Gary spelled "onomatopoeia." The word list in Ms. Ionescu's hand grew thinner with every round, and Florence could see it, a shrinking stack, until there was only one card left.

"Gary, your word is 'serendipity.'"

Gary spelled it right, and Ms. Ionescu looked at the empty stack, then at the two of them. "That's the end of the list," she said. "Florence, you'll take one word from the backup envelope, and Gary the next. If you both get them right, I'll need to check the rules."

Florence took her card. "Momentous," Ms. Ionescu said.

"M-O-M-E-N-T-O-U-S," said Florence.

Ms. Ionescu smiled and reached for her phone. "Clarissa, come read me the third bullet on that bee article. I want to hear it again."

Clarissa stood up, grinning, and read, "In 2019, the Scripps National Spelling Bee crowned eight co-champions."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
Lucas was sitting on Graydon's bedroom floor with Graydon's phone, hunting for an old joke video the two of them had watched about fifty times in fifth grade. The channel that had posted it seemed to be gone. Every search just returned reuploads and dead links. "It has to be somewhere," Graydon said, bouncing a tennis ball off the wall. "The internet keeps everything, right?" Lucas was skeptical about that, because he had lost enough saved games to know that things on screens disappeared all the time. But he kept typing, and on the fourth try he landed on a page he had never seen before. At the top it said Internet Archive, and it claimed that since 1996 it had been saving copies of public web pages.

"That can't be real," Lucas said. Graydon leaned over his shoulder. Under the words was a search box, and Lucas typed in the address of their old school's website, the one that had been redone last year. The page loaded a version from years ago, complete with a photo of the class of that year standing in front of the gym, every face clear and labeled with first names.

Graydon went quiet in a way he almost never did. "Wait. Try my cousin's old blog," he said. "She had one in elementary school and she deleted it, like, forever ago." Lucas typed it in, half expecting a blank error page. Instead the old blog appeared, pink background and all, with a post about a family trip, and, at the bottom, a note about exactly which beach house they had rented, down to the street. "Anyone could read this," Graydon said slowly. "Anyone in the world. Strangers. It's still just sitting there." Lucas scrolled further and found a post full of photos, each one tagged with the park where they had been taken, and the day, and even the time.

"It's like the page is insulated from deleting," Lucas said. "You take it down, but this copy just sits there protected." Then a thought hit him, and his stomach did a small flip. In fifth grade he had kept a blog too, before he knew better, and he had posted a picture of his own house with the street sign visible. He had deleted it two years ago and never thought about it again. His intuition said this archive thing would not have it, because his blog had been tiny and nobody read it. But he had been wrong before.

"Graydon. My blog." He typed his old address with his thumb hovering, almost hoping for an error. The pink and blue page of his eleven-year-old self loaded instantly, complete with the photo of the house, the street sign, and a post that began "Nobody probably reads this but." He stared at it. Then he started copying down the archive's contact page, because it had a link for asking to have things removed. "It might not work," Graydon said. Lucas nodded. "Only one way to find out." He tapped the button that said submit.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A batting average is hits divided by official at-bats, and walks do not count as at-bats, so the number gives a batter no credit for walks.
story:
Olivier had saved the ranking page on his phone two weeks ago, and every day it bothered him the same way. His favorite player, the one with the strange high leg kick, sat forty-third in the league. Forty-third. Olivier thought he was top ten, and tonight, in the bleachers waiting for Kathleen and Leighton before the game started, he planned to prove it.

"Forty-third is forty-third," Kathleen said, unwrapping a granola bar. "The numbers don't lie."

"The numbers are missing things," Olivier said. "Watch this." He opened his notebook, where he had copied the player's season line by hand. "Look. Hits divided by official at-bats, that's the batting average. But walks don't count as at-bats." He tapped the page. "So a walk gives a batter no credit. None. He gets on base and the average just sits there."

Leighton frowned at the math. "That can't be right. Getting on base helps the team."

Olivier tested it with small numbers right there on the notebook page, because he didn't want to just believe it. Two hits in four at-bats was .500, great. But if the player walked his next three times up, the average stayed .250, because those walks were not at-bats at all. He pushed the notebook toward Kathleen. "He's aggressive at the plate," Olivier said. "Pitchers are scared of him, so they walk him. The ranking punishes him for it."

The gym buzzer went off and the teams ran out. Kathleen chewed slowly, watching the point guard, whose picture Olivier had also printed and taped inside the notebook cover. She had enrolled her in the same fan club Olivier joined in September, before the player got good and the trouble started.

"He should still be higher," she said finally. "You're counting the walks on top of the hits. The average isn't."

Olivier felt his conscience poke him a little, because he had argued the same wrong thing yesterday, that the average must include everything. He had gone home and checked. It didn't.

"Fine," Kathleen said. "I'll write him a letter too."

The point guard drove baseline, got fouled, and stepped to the line while the crowd stomped the bleachers. Olivier held up his notebook so the section could see the cover, and Leighton started the chant first.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: A ball rolling on a flat floor gradually slows down because friction and rolling resistance take away its energy.
story:
Justin knelt at the end of the hallway with a stopwatch, a tennis ball, and a sheet of graph paper that Ms. Sánchez had appointed him to fill in by Monday. The assignment said to measure the speed of a rolling ball, time how long it took to travel a known distance, and draw a distance-time graph. He had put it off all weekend, and now it was Sunday afternoon and the graph was still blank.

He set two pieces of tape on the tile floor, three meters apart, and crouched to push the ball gently from the first mark. He clicked the stopwatch as it crossed each one. Faster than he expected. He did it again, then again, and wrote the numbers in the margin. When he tried to plot them, the points scattered instead of forming a coherent line, and he sat back on his heels, frowning at the paper.

Oceane had done her graph on Friday, he remembered, while he was playing video games. She had asked if he wanted to time it with her, and he had said later. He looked down the empty hallway and thought about that choice for a moment, then got up and went to find his older cousin, who was visiting and reading in the den.

His cousin suggested more intervals. So Justin laid tape every half meter, seven marks in all, and rolled the ball while he ran alongside clicking the stopwatch. Something odd appeared in his numbers. The ball covered the first half meter in almost no time, but each later stretch took longer, until the last stretch took more than twice as long as the first. He checked the ball. Nothing was wrong with it. He rolled it again and watched it the whole way, and this time he saw it plainly: it was still slowing down when it crossed the final mark.

He thought about the ball his grandfather used to keep in the garage, a heavy rubber one that had been handed down like some descendant of an old bowling set, and how it had always stopped short on the mat by the door but rolled forever on the concrete. He looked from the tile to the living room, where the floor turned to carpet. He rolled the ball onto the rug and it stopped within a arm's length, dead, as if it had run out of something.

Back in the hallway, he rolled the ball twice more, wrote the times, and connected the dots. The line climbed steeply and then bent, flattening as it went. He stared at it, then leaned close to the tile and watched the next roll slow, halfway down the hall, still turning, and slowing all the time. "There it is," he said to the empty hallway.

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: In Leonardo da Vinci's Last Supper, the single vanishing point is at Christ's head, and a nail hole Leonardo used to stretch his guide strings is still visible there.
story:
Harrison pressed his pencil so hard against the paper that the street he was drawing began to look like it had been through a storm. Every building leaned the wrong way, and the road refused to narrow into the distance. Ms. Banerjee walked past his desk and tapped the spot where the road should have gone. "Pick your vanishing point first," she said. "Every line that runs away from you has to aim straight at it."

"That's it?" Dylan whispered from the next seat. "One dot controls the whole street?" Harrison stared at his paper. It seemed strange that something invisible, a point that wasn't a real object at all, could be in charge of every edge of every building. He erased his messy lines and tried again, starting with a single dot near the top of the page. The edges of the road aimed at it. The rooftops aimed at it. Slowly the street flattened itself into depth, as if the paper had opened a window.

At lunch he couldn't stop thinking about it. If one hidden point could organize a whole picture, had artists always done this? In the library he found a thick book about Leonardo da Vinci and flipped through it until a page about the Last Supper stopped him cold. He read the paragraph twice, then a third time. "Aleksandra," he called across the table, "come look at this." He waited until she pulled her chair over. "In the Last Supper, the vanishing point is right at Christ's head. And there's a nail hole there, from strings Leonardo stretched to make his guide lines. You can still see it."

Aleksandra leaned in, squinting at the painting. "A nail hole? In one of the most famous paintings on earth?" She sounded as amazed as he felt. "So the whole room in that picture, the walls, the ceiling, the windows, they all point at his head?" Harrison ran his finger along the lines in the book's reproduction, and sure enough, every edge of the room flowed toward that single point. It was like discovering the wire behind a magic trick.

Back in art class, he had an idea and, feeling impulsive, he acted on it before he could talk himself out of anything. He asked Ms. Banerjee for a pin and a length of thread, then pinned one end of the thread exactly at his vanishing point. When he swung the thread across the page, it lay perfectly along his street's edges, his rooftops, his sidewalk. "What's the probability my lines are this straight by accident?" he asked Aleksandra, who had wandered over to watch. She shook her head slowly. "Zero," she said. Harrison grinned and swung the thread again, watching it sweep across his little street like the hand of a clock.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Italian tempo words describe speed: largo means very slow, andante means at a walking pace, and allegro means fast and lively.
story:
The concert hall smelled like dust and lemon polish, and Savannah's hands were already sweating on her sheet music. In three weeks she would play the middle section of "River Song" on the school piano while Winnie played flute beside her, and Ms. Koné had written one word at the top of the page that was ruining everything: andante.

"What does that even mean?" Winnie whispered, leaning over the music stand on the diagonal aisle that cut from the stage door to the front row.

Savannah had a guess. Italian words looked fancy, and fancy meant fast, at least in her head. "Fast, I think. Like, show-off fast." She set the metronome racing, threw her fingers at the keys, and collaborated with Winnie the only way she knew how, which was to play louder and faster until the melody crashed into the flute part and both of them stopped, breathing hard. The piece had fallen apart, torn right down the middle.

From the third row, Loralie laughed, then covered her mouth. "Sorry. But that was so wrong. My grandma plays this stuff." She hopped up onto the stage edge. "She says largo means very slow. Like syrup."

"Then andante must be slow too," Savannah said, frowning at the page. But that did not fit either, because the next section was marked allegro, and surely the whole piece was not slow, slow, slow. She thought about the words themselves. Largo, she decided, was the slowest. Allegro sounded bright, quick, happy. That left andante sitting in the middle, and she remembered that in her cousin's old exercise book there had been a note next to it, a little drawing of a person strolling down a sidewalk. Walking. Andante meant walking pace, not slow, not racing. She had skipped past it because it seemed too ordinary to matter.

"Let's test it," she said. "Walking speed, but not dragging." She reset the metronome to a steady, unhurried tick, and this time she let the dynamics do the work instead of speed. Soft where the page said piano, swelling where it said crescendo, her hands crossing over each other as the line climbed. Winnie's flute slid in under the melody like it had been waiting there all along. When they reached the allegro, they leapt together, and it felt less like playing and more like flying.

Ms. Koné stood at the back of the hall with her arms folded, and when the last note faded she called out, "Again. Same tempo. More shape."

"Warranty on that?" Winnie asked, grinning.

"None," said Ms. Koné. "Musicians break constantly."

Savannah laughed, flexed her fingers, and set the metronome ticking.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Noah Webster's 1828 'American Dictionary of the English Language' promoted simpler spellings such as 'color' instead of 'colour', which became standard in the United States.
story:
The auditorium smelled like floor wax and nervous popcorn, even though nobody was allowed to eat in there. Alexis stood in line with eleven other spellers, holding her number card like a shield, and next to her Teresa was bouncing on her toes.

"I've got a secret weapon," Teresa whispered. "My cousin in Canada sends me words. She says Americans spell half of them wrong."

"That's not possible," Alexis said, but her stomach went tight. What if it was? The judge, Ms. Farah-Ali, called the first speller, and a boy got out on "restaurant," and the audience did that sad murmur, and Alexis thought about nothing but letters.

Round four, Teresa drew a word and grinned. "Colour. C-O-L-O-U-R." The bell dinged, wrong. Teresa froze. "That's how my cousin spells it! She writes it in every letter!"

"That's the Canadian way," Ms. Farah-Ali said gently. "In the United States we drop the u." Teresa walked offstage, and Alexis felt weird, half glad and half furious on her friend's behalf. Somebody had to be right, but who decided? She budgeted her remaining brainpower carefully: half for her own turns, half for this mystery.

Between rounds, Alexis tested a simple idea. She asked the next three eliminated spellers what they'd missed. "Honour," said one. "Favourite," said another. Every single one had that sneaky u. It was a pattern, like a trap set on purpose. At lunch Alexis had read the dictionary's front pages, hunting for gossip, and she'd found an anecdote about Noah Webster and his 1828 American Dictionary of the English Language. He promoted simpler spellings like "color" instead of "colour," and those became standard in the United States. It wasn't a mistake or a mystery. One man, one dictionary, one country that followed him. Canada just kept the older spelling. Alexis wanted to leap up and tell everyone, but Ms. Farah-Ali was already calling the final round.

Alexis stepped to the microphone, hesitant for exactly one second, then steady. Her word was "neighbor." Teresa's cousin would add a u, and Alexis knew exactly why, and exactly who to thank.

"N-E-I-G-H-B-O-R. Neighbor."

The bell stayed silent. The audience roared, and somewhere in the third row Teresa shouted, "Tell my cousin it was Webster's fault!"

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A settler's diary shows one person's view; it rarely tells how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events.
story:
Isla slid the photocopied diary pages across the library table like they were top secret files, which, in her opinion, they nearly were. "This is a real settler's diary from the 1800s," she whispered. "The actual words of a guy walking a wagon trail west. Ms. Whitehead says it's a primary source, so we can build our whole poster on it."

Wynter leaned over, scanning the cramped handwriting. "He complains about the mud for three pages. Three. Pages. Of mud."

"He crossed a whole continent. I think he earned his complaining," Isla said. "This is perfect for why people moved west. He writes about land, and starting over, and how his old town couldn't accommodate their whole family on one small farm." She tapped the word like a game show buzzer. "Evidence!"

Aliza arrived late, breathless, carrying her own notebook. "I found something too. Not a diary. A speech. From one of the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed. A chief talking about wagons rolling through their territory." She set it down between them. "It's a different view of the exact same events."

Isla stared at the two documents side by side. "Wait. So the diary says the trail was empty land waiting for them, and the speech says the land already belonged to people?"

"Yep." Aliza popped the p. "The diary shows one person's view. It rarely tells how the nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events."

"So my poster is only half the story." Isla sat back, feeling the whole project tip over in her head. Then she grabbed a marker and flipped the poster board sideways, drawing a wide brown line down the middle. "New plan. This is the trail. Diary quotes on one side, the chief's words on the other. Same trail, two views."

"That's actually brilliant," Wynter admitted, then pointed at Isla's title, which read WESTWARD HO. "But you have to change that title."

"It's a classic."

"It's a snooze." Wynter snatched the marker and wrote TWO SIDES OF ONE TRAIL, grinning in a way that was frankly contagious, because Isla caught herself grinning back even while defending her honor.

When Ms. Whitehead stopped at their table later, she read both columns, then looked up. "Whose idea was the split poster?"

"Mine," said Isla, "but Aliza found the second source, and Wynter mocked my title."

"A team effort," said Wynter, patting the poster. "My heritage is merciless editing."

Ms. Whitehead laughed and moved on, and Isla bent over the board to letter the chief's words carefully onto the left side, marker squeaking the whole way down.
